c.tagline: A living medieval maze of tanneries, madrasas and the world's oldest university.

taxi.fareNote: Fès uses red petits taxis for short in-city hops (insist on the meter, or compteur) and cream grands taxis for airport runs and longer trips. There are no international ride-hailing apps in Fès, so hail on the street or ask your riad to call one; the old medina is car-free, so taxis only reach its gates.

emergency.note: Dial 19 for police and 15 for ambulance/fire (Protection Civile). Outside cities and on highways, 177 reaches the Gendarmerie Royale.

avoid.reason: Fake guides and hassle in the medina — use licensed guides; easy to get lost

hood_desc: The vast car-free medieval old city and a UNESCO World Heritage site, often called the world's largest car-free urban area, with the Al-Qarawiyyin university-mosque, the Chouara tanneries, the Bou Inania madrasa and a maze of thousands of lanes; best for first-timers who want to sleep inside a living medieval city in a converted riad.

The 'new' Marinid-era walled city west of the old medina, holding the Royal Palace's golden gates, the Mellah (historic Jewish quarter) and the Bab Semmarine market street; quieter and more spread out than Fes el-Bali, good for history without the deepest medina crowds.

The French-built modern district of wide boulevards, the train station, international-brand hotels, bars and contemporary restaurants; suits travelers who want modern comforts, nightlife and easy transport over medieval atmosphere.

The transitional quarter just outside Bab Bou Jeloud (the Blue Gate) around the Batha Museum, packed with riads, cafes and the main medina gateway; a convenient, walkable base straddling the old and new cities.

A calm, leafy residential and administrative district in the newer city with gardens, apartment blocks and local eateries; suits longer-stay and budget travelers wanting a quieter, everyday-local feel away from the tourist core.

water.note: City tap is chlorinated, but most visitors stick to bottled.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 9:00 PM; red petits taxis fill the late-night gaps.
transit.note: Fès has no metro or tram; the Alsa city bus network and red petits taxis are the main transport. The old medina (Fes el-Bali) is entirely car-free, so within it you walk or hire a porter with a handcart.
transit.pay: Pay bus fares in cash to the driver (a few dirhams). Petits taxis are metered by law; insist on the compteur.

train: ONCF national rail (Fès station) to Casablanca, Rabat, Marrakech, Tangier and Oujda

transit.m: Airport bus (Line 16) to the city center / train station (~30-40 min)
Grand taxi to the medina or Ville Nouvelle (20-25 min)

tip.r: Round up or leave 5-10% at restaurants; a few dirhams for cafe staff, guides and porters is customary.

food.name: Pastilla
food.desc: Fes's signature pie: shredded pigeon or chicken with almonds, egg and cinnamon layered in paper-thin warqa pastry and dusted with icing sugar.

places.name: Cafe Restaurant Al Oud
places.note: Bright medina cafe widely rated for its pastilla and lamb tagine at fair 70-85 dirham prices.

places.name: Darori
places.note: Zellij-tiled dining room celebrating Fassi classics, including a proper pigeon pastilla.

places.name: The Ruined Garden
places.note: Courtyard restaurant in a crumbling riad; refined pastilla in one of the medina's prettiest settings.

food.name: Harira
food.desc: Tomato, lentil and chickpea soup thickened with flour and sharpened with lemon and coriander; the everyday bowl and the Ramadan fast-breaker.

places.name: Bab Boujloud food stalls
places.note: Cauldrons of harira ladled out beside the blue gate from late afternoon; cheapest and most authentic.

places.name: Cafe Clock
places.note: Long-established medina cafe in a converted house; dependable harira and a good first stop for newcomers.

places.name: Nagham Cafe
places.note: Rooftop terrace two minutes from the blue gate with medina views over a bowl of soup.

food.name: Kefta tagine
food.desc: Spiced beef or lamb meatballs simmered in tomato and cumin sauce with eggs cracked in at the end, mopped up with khobz bread.

places.name: Cafe Restaurant Al Oud
places.note: Simple, generous tagines cooked to order in the heart of the old city.

places.name: Dar Hatim
places.note: Family home-restaurant serving Fassi cooking as the household actually eats it; book ahead.

places.name: Nagham Cafe
places.note: Reliable kefta tagine with a view; handy after a morning in the tanneries.

food.name: Sfenj
food.desc: Rings of sticky dough deep-fried to order until crisp outside and airy inside, then threaded on palm string and eaten hot with sugar or honey.

places.name: Bab Boujloud sfenj stalls
places.note: Fryers work the morning shift by the blue gate; buy them straight off the string.

places.name: Talaa Kebira morning stands
places.note: Several sfenj men work the main artery at breakfast; follow the queue of locals.

places.name: Place R'cif stalls
places.note: Lower-medina square where sfenj is fried alongside msemen and mint tea.

food.name: Mechoui
food.desc: Whole lamb shoulder rubbed with cumin and butter and roasted for hours until it pulls apart; served with bread, cumin and salt on the side.

places.name: Palais Amani - The Garden
places.note: Riad restaurant known for a seven-hour lamb mechoui served in the courtyard garden.

places.name: The Ruined Garden
places.note: Slow-roast lamb needs ordering a day ahead; worth it for the setting alone.

places.name: Bab Boujloud grill stalls
places.note: Street grills carve roast lamb and brochettes to order for a fraction of restaurant prices.

food.name: Fassi couscous
food.desc: The Friday dish: hand-rolled semolina steamed over a broth of lamb or chicken with seven vegetables, caramelised onion and chickpeas.

places.name: Dar Hatim
places.note: Home-cooked Friday couscous served in a family riad; reserve in advance.

places.name: Dar Roumana
places.note: Riad kitchen with medina views doing a carefully built Fassi couscous.

places.name: Cafe Clock
places.note: Easy walk-in option for couscous on Fridays without a reservation.

food.name: Mint tea
food.desc: Atay bi na'na: gunpowder green tea steeped with a bundle of fresh spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from height to raise a foam.

places.name: Cafe Clock
places.note: Known for its mint tea and Moroccan pastries; shaded terrace above the medina lanes.

places.name: The Ruined Garden
places.note: Afternoon tea from homegrown mint and wormwood in a garden of fountains and mosaics.

places.name: Nagham Cafe
places.note: Rooftop glasses of mint tea with a full view over the old city rooftops.

food.name: Fresh juice and jus d'avocat
food.desc: Medina juice carts squeeze oranges to order and blend the Moroccan avocado shake with milk, almonds, dates and orange-flower water.

places.name: Bab Boujloud juice stalls
places.note: Orange presses run all day at the gate; the avocado shakes are thick enough to eat.

places.name: Place R'cif juice carts
places.note: Local-priced juices in the lower medina where fewer tourists reach.

places.name: Place Seffarine cafes
places.note: Sit with a juice among the coppersmiths hammering trays; a classic medina pause.

landmarks: Fes el-Bali (Old Medina)
A UNESCO-listed medieval labyrinth of 9,000 car-free alleys, this world's largest urban pedestrian zone overwhelms the senses with donkeys, artisans and centuries-old workshops.
Bab Boujloud (The Blue Gate)
The medina's iconic 1913 gateway glitters with blue zellij tiles facing outward and green within, framing a postcard view of minarets and market bustle.
Al Quaraouiyine Mosque and University
Founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, this working mosque houses what UNESCO calls the world's oldest continuously operating university, its green-tiled roofs crowning the medina.
Chouara Tannery
From leather-shop terraces, gaze down on a honeycomb of medieval stone vats where hides are dyed in saffron, poppy and indigo exactly as they were centuries ago.
Bou Inania Madrasa
This 14th-century Marinid theological college dazzles with carved cedar, intricate stucco and zellij mosaics, and is one of few religious sites open to non-Muslims.
Al-Attarine Madrasa
Tucked beside the spice market, this jewel-box 1325 madrasa concentrates the finest Marinid craftsmanship in Morocco into one exquisitely tiled and carved courtyard.
Marinid Tombs
These ruined 14th-century hilltop mausoleums offer the classic sunset panorama over Fes el-Bali's sea of rooftops, minarets and drifting tannery smoke.
Nejjarine Fountain and Museum of Wooden Arts
A gorgeously tiled 18th-century fountain fronts a restored funduq caravanserai whose galleried courtyard now displays Morocco's finest antique woodwork and craft tools.
Zaouia of Moulay Idriss II
The green-roofed shrine of Fez's 9th-century founder is the city's holiest site, its brass-studded doors and pilgrims' candles glimpsed from surrounding alleys.
Royal Palace Gates (Dar el-Makhzen)
Seven monumental brass doors framed by zellij and carved cedar make the entrance to the king's Fez palace one of Morocco's most photographed facades.

train.note: No international trains. Fes station is a 20-minute walk from the Ville Nouvelle and connects to Casablanca in about 3h30, Rabat in 2h40 and Tangier in 4 with a change at Sidi Kacem or via the high-speed link. Trains east to Oujda near the Algerian border take 6 hours, but the frontier itself is closed. Book on the ONCF site or app for advance fares.

bus.note: International coaches route via Tanger Med and the Spain ferry, taking a day or more. Domestically CTM (https://www.ctm.ma/) and Supratours (https://www.supratours.ma/) run to Chefchaouen in about 4 hours - the main reason to take the bus here, as there is no train - plus Merzouga and the Middle Atlas towns. Buy online or at the CTM terminal rather than the chaotic gare routière.

ferry.note: Fes is inland in northern Morocco with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. The nearest crossings to Spain are from Tangier and Tanger Med, about four hours away by train.

half.name: Volubilis & Meknes
half.blurb: Well-preserved Roman ruins with mosaic floors near Meknes, one of Morocco's four imperial cities and a royal granary.

half.name: Ifrane
half.blurb: Alpine-style resort town in the Middle Atlas cedar forests, sometimes called Little Switzerland for its architecture.

full.name: Chefchaouen
full.blurb: Mountain town of blue-washed alleys in the Rif range, a roughly three-hour drive north of Fès.
